la:noun:ara.html:
āra, ae, f. (Osc. form aasa; Umbr. asa: PELLEX. ASAM. IVNONIS. NE. TAGITO., Lex Numae ap. ; cf. ; ) [perh. Sanscr. ās, Gr. ἧμαι, Dor. ἧσμαι = to sit, as the seat or resting-place of the victim or offering; v. ],
an altar.
Lit.: Jovis aram sanguine turpari, Enn. ap. (Trag. v. 125 Vahl.): Inde ignem in aram, ut Ephesiae Dianae laeta laudes,: omnīs accedere ad aras ... aras sanguine multo Spargere,; so : turicremas aras, (adopted by ); 2, 417: multo sanguine maesti Conspergunt aras adolentque altaria donis,: ara Aio Loquenti consecrata,: ara condita atque dicata,; cf. : ara sacrata,; cf. : exstruere,; so : construere,: facere,: erigere,: aedificare,: ponere,: destruere,, and : subvertere,: dissipare,: suffodere,: demolire,: depopulari, ib. Osee, 10, 2: interibunt arae vestrae, et saep.—Altars were erected not only in the temples, but also in the streets and highways, in the open air, .—Esp. were altars erected in the courts of houses (impluvia), for the family gods (Penates), while the household gods (Lares) received offerings upon a small hearth (focus) in the family hall (atrium); hence, arae et foci, meton. for home, or hearth and home, and pro aris et focis pugnare, to fight for altars and fires, for one's dearest possessions: urbem, agrum, aras, focos seque dedere,: te amicum Deiotari regis arae focique viderunt,: de vestris conjugibus ac liberis, de aris ac focis, decernite,; : nos domicilia, sedesque populi Romani, Penates, aras, focos, sepulcra majorum defendimus,: patriae, parentibus, aris atque focis bellum parare,: pro patriā, pro liberis, pro aris atque focis suis cernere,: sibi pro aris focisque et deūm templis ac solo, in quo nati essent, dimicandum fore, et saep.—Criminals fled to the altars for protection, Don. ad : interim hanc aram occupabo,: Priamum cum in aram confugisset, hostilis manus interemit,: eo ille confugit in arāque consedit,: Veneris sanctae considam vinctus ad aras: haec supplicibus favet,.—Hence, trop., protection, refuge, shelter: tamquam in aram confugitis ad deum,: ad aram legum confugere,: hic portus, haec ara sociorum,; ; ; ; .—One who took an oath was accustomed to lay hold of the altar, in confirmation of it, : qui si aram tenens juraret, crederet nemo,; (cf. ): tango aras, medios ignes et numina testor,; : ara sepulcri, a funeral pile, regarded as an altar, ; .—
Meton.
The Altar, a constellation in the southern sky, Gr. Θυτήριον (Arat. 403 al.): Aram, quam flatu permulcet spiritus austri, poët. ap. ; so ; Orell.; , and : pressa,i. e. low in the south,. —
Arae, The Altars.
Rocky cliffs in the Mediterranean Sea, between Sicily Sardinia and Africa, so called from their shape, Varr. ap. ; Quadrig. Ann. ib.: saxa vocant Itali, mediis quae in fluctibus, Aras,.—
Arae Philaenorum, v. Philaeni.—
Transf., in gen., a monument of stone: ara virtutis,: Lunensis ara,of Lunensian marble,—Also

a tombstone: ARAM D. S. P. R. (de suā pecuniā restituit),; so ; .

senses: ploughman or plowman, farmer, husbandman (someone that ploughs/plows)
la:noun:arator.html:
ărātor, ōris, m.
aro
.
Lit., one that ploughs, a ploughman; freq. poet. = agricola, a husbandman, farmer, : caput quassans grandis suspirat arator Crebrius, * : luce sacrā requiescat arator,: Concidere infelix validos miratur arator Inter opus tauros,; ; : neque jam stabulis gaudet pecus aut aratorigni, * et saep.—Adj.: taurus arator,: bos arator,; v. Zumpt, § 102.—
In the Rom. lang. of finance, aratores, the cultivators of public lands for a tenth of the produce; cf. aratio, II. (usu. the Roman knights): aratorum penuria,; so ; 2, 2, 13; 2, 2, 64; 2, 3, 20; 2, 3, 27; 2, 3, 50; ; ; .—
Meton., The Ploughman, a constellation, Nigid. and Varr. ap. .

la:other:Arabia.html:
Ā^răbĭa (on account of the long A in , erroneously written by many Arrabia; cf. Jahn ad ), ae, f., = Ἀραβία.
In an extended sense, the country Arabia, divided by the ancients into Petrœa (from its principal city, Petra), Deserta, and Felix, ; ; ; —
In a more restricted sense, a town in Arabia Felix, . —Hence, ā^răbĭcus, a, um, adj., Arabic, Arabian: odor (i. e. tus),: sinus,; : resina,: adamas,: alites,: balanus,: lapicidinae, i. e. of alabaster,: spina,the acacia,: vectis,. 17. —Absol.: ā^răbĭca, ae, f. (sc. gemma), a precious stone, similar to ivory, perh. a kind of chalcedony or onyx, ; .—ā^răbĭcē, adv.: facite olant aedes Arabice, make the apartments redolent with the perfumes of Araby (frankincense, which was brought from Arabia), Plaut. ap. P. (Arabice olet, id est ex odoribus Arabicis, ): Arabice sacri vocantur, in Arabic, Sol. c. 33.

ărānĕa, ae, f.

A spider's web, cobweb: (aedes) oppletae araneis,: ut aranea bratteaque auri,: arcula plena aranearum, Afran. ap. Fest. s. v. tanne, p. 154 Müll. (Com. Rel. p. 217 Rib.): Catulli Plenus sacculus est aranearum,: summo quae pendet aranea tigno,; .—
Also, for threads similar to spiders' webs: salicis fructus ante maturitatem in araneam abit,.

la:noun:aratio.html:
ărātĭo, ōnis, f.
aro

A ploughing, and in gen. the cultivation of the ground, agriculture: iteratio arationis peracta esse debet, si, etc.,: aratione per transversum iterata,: ut quaestuosa mercatura, fructuosa aratio dicitur,.—
